title: New diagnosis of type 2 diabetes
candidate: You are a GP. Your patient, a 52-year-old office manager, has come for the results of a routine blood test.
A repeat HbA1c of 62 mmol/mol confirms type 2 diabetes.
Find out what the patient already knows about diabetes.
Explain the diagnosis in plain language.
Respond to the patient's worry about insulin: most people start with lifestyle changes and tablets.
Outline the next steps: metformin, diet, activity, a diabetes education course and a review in three months.
otherParty: You are a 52-year-old office manager. You feel well and expected a normal result.
Your father had diabetes, needed insulin and later lost a foot. You are frightened.
At first you do not really listen; you keep asking whether you will need injections.
You calm down if the doctor explains clearly and asks about your concerns.
You worry about fitting exercise into long working days.

title: A parent asking for antibiotics
candidate: You are a GP. A parent has brought their 4-year-old daughter, who has had a cough, runny nose and a temperature of 38 °C for two days.
On examination, the child is alert, drinking well, with a red throat and clear chest. This is a viral infection.
Find out the parent's main concern.
Explain why antibiotics would not help and could cause side effects.
Advise on fluids, paracetamol or ibuprofen, and rest.
Give clear safety-netting advice: when to come back or seek urgent help.
otherParty: You are the child's parent. You have missed two days of work and need your daughter back at nursery.
Last winter, antibiotics seemed to help your son quickly.
You insist on antibiotics and become irritated if you feel dismissed.
You accept the plan if the doctor listens to you and gives clear advice about warning signs.
You want to know how long the illness will last.

title: A patient afraid of contrast for a CT scan
candidate: You are a doctor in the radiology department. A 60-year-old patient is booked for a CT scan of the abdomen with contrast to investigate weight loss.
The patient has told the radiographer they do not want the contrast injection.
Find out why the patient is worried.
Explain why contrast is needed and what it involves (a warm feeling, a metallic taste).
Explain the risk of a reaction: serious reactions are rare, and the team is trained to treat them.
Ask about any previous reaction to contrast. Explain what can be done: precautions such as premedication or a different contrast agent, or a scan without contrast, which shows less.
Respect the patient's decision and agree a way forward.
otherParty: You are 60 years old. Years ago you had an itchy rash after an X-ray dye; nobody told you what it was.
A friend told you contrast can damage the kidneys.
You are anxious and want to leave without the scan.
You agree to the scan if the doctor explains the risks honestly and offers precautions.
You want to know whether the scan can be done without contrast.

title: Consent for a CT-guided lung biopsy
candidate: You are a doctor in interventional radiology. A 67-year-old patient has a 2.5 cm nodule in the right lung, and a CT-guided biopsy is planned for today.
Check what the patient understands about the procedure.
Explain the procedure: local anaesthetic, a thin needle, lying still for about 30 minutes.
Explain the main risks: a collapsed lung (pneumothorax) in about 1 in 5, usually minor; coughing up a little blood.
Answer the patient's question about cancer honestly, without guessing the result.
Check understanding and ask whether the patient is happy to go ahead.
otherParty: You are 67 years old and have smoked all your life. You are sure the nodule is cancer.
You are frightened of needles and of being awake during the procedure.
You keep asking the doctor to tell you whether it is cancer.
You want to know whether you can drive home afterwards.
You agree to the biopsy if you feel the doctor is honest and patient with you.

title: Stopping smoking after a heart attack
candidate: You are a doctor on the cardiology ward. A 55-year-old builder had a heart attack three days ago and had a stent. He will go home tomorrow.
He smokes 20 cigarettes a day.
Find out how he feels about his smoking.
Explain how smoking affects his heart and the stent.
Offer support: nicotine replacement or varenicline, and the local stop-smoking service.
Agree a realistic plan with him.
otherParty: You are a 55-year-old builder. You have smoked since you were 15.
You have tried to stop twice and failed; you feel ashamed about it.
At first you say smoking is the only way you cope with stress.
You become more open if the doctor does not lecture you.
You are worried about gaining weight if you stop.

title: MRI shows a disc prolapse — surgery is not needed yet
candidate: You are a GP. A 41-year-old teacher has had sciatica down the left leg for five weeks. The MRI shows an L5/S1 disc prolapse. There is no weakness and no bladder or bowel problem.
Go through the MRI result with the patient.
Explain that most disc prolapses improve without surgery within weeks to months.
Explain the plan: pain relief, staying active, physiotherapy.
Explain the warning signs that need urgent help (numbness in the saddle area, bladder or bowel problems, new weakness).
Agree when to review and when surgery might be considered.
otherParty: You are a 41-year-old teacher. You have read online that a disc prolapse needs an operation.
You expect to be referred to a surgeon today and feel disappointed.
You are struggling to stand in class all day.
You ask for a fit note.
You accept the plan if the doctor explains why surgery is not the first step.

title: A patient asking for a scan for back pain
candidate: You are a GP. A 35-year-old warehouse worker has had low back pain for ten days after lifting. There are no red flags and the examination is normal.
The patient is asking for an MRI scan.
Find out why the patient wants a scan.
Explain why a scan would not change the treatment at this stage.
Advise on staying active, simple pain relief and safe lifting.
Explain when you would arrange a scan.
otherParty: You are a 35-year-old warehouse worker. Your employer needs to know when you can return.
You believe something must be broken, because the pain is so bad.
You feel the doctor is not taking you seriously if no scan is offered.
You calm down if the doctor explains what the examination showed.
You ask whether you should rest in bed.

title: Going home after an asthma attack
candidate: You are a doctor in the emergency department. A 24-year-old student came in with an asthma attack and has improved after treatment.
The patient uses only a blue reliever inhaler, sometimes several times a day.
Find out how the patient uses their inhalers.
Explain the difference between the preventer and the reliever inhaler.
Explain the prednisolone course for five days.
Explain the warning signs of a severe attack and arrange a GP review within two days.
otherParty: You are a 24-year-old student. You stopped your brown preventer inhaler because you felt fine.
You worry that steroids will make you gain weight.
You have exams next week and want to go home quickly.
You did not realise the attack was serious.
You agree to the plan if it is explained simply.

title: An angry daughter: surgery delayed
candidate: You are a doctor on the orthopaedic ward. An 84-year-old woman with a hip fracture was admitted 30 hours ago. Her operation was postponed today because a more urgent case needed theatre.
Her daughter has asked to speak to a doctor.
Acknowledge the daughter's feelings and apologise for the delay.
Explain the reason for the delay.
Explain what is being done to keep her mother comfortable and safe (pain relief, fluids, pressure care).
Explain the plan: the operation is first on tomorrow's list.
otherParty: You are the patient's daughter. Your mother has been without food since last night and is in pain.
You were told this morning that she would have surgery today.
You are angry at first and say you will make a complaint.
You calm down if the doctor listens, apologises and explains honestly.
You want to know whether the delay is dangerous for your mother.

title: Starting a blood thinner for atrial fibrillation
candidate: You are a GP. A 72-year-old patient has newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation. You recommend apixaban to reduce the risk of stroke.
Find out what the patient already knows about atrial fibrillation.
Explain the link between atrial fibrillation and stroke.
Explain the benefits and risks of apixaban, including bleeding.
Explain the signs of serious bleeding and what to do.
Check understanding and support the patient in making a decision.
otherParty: You are 72 and still play golf twice a week.
Your neighbour had a bad bleed on warfarin, and you are reluctant to take a blood thinner.
You feel well and do not understand why you need tablets.
You ask whether you can stop the tablet if you get a nosebleed.
You would like time to think and to talk to your wife.
